# Sif: canonical, contested, and the false forms on record

*Evidence dossier 483 — Sif. Every exhibit catalogued, every ruling stated with its grounds.*

## At a Glance

- **Canonical form:** Sif
- **Reconstructed form:** ᛋᛁᚠ (a normalized scholarly specimen)
- **Pantheon:** Norse
- **Convention:** the tradition's scholarly romanization, kept exactly as recorded
- **False forms on record:** 0
- **Contested forms:** none attested
- **Series:** The Canonical Register, No. 483 of 597

## The Evidence

**Exhibit 1 — the attestation.** The reconstructed form is **ᛋᛁᚠ** — a normalized scholarly specimen, not an attested inscription. The canonical transliteration is **Sif**.

**Exhibit 2 — the flattened form.** The plain form *sif* differs from the canonical **Sif** only by convention of display — case, not content. It is **acceptable everywhere**: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

**Exhibit 3 — the physical record.** Sif is a wholly textual goddess: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit names her, and no image can be securely identified with her — a silence she shares with most of the ásynjur, who appear in verse and prose but rarely, if ever, in dedications. Her attestation hangs on the manuscript witnesses of the two Eddas: the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda for Lokasenna and Hárbarðsljóð, and the Codex Regius and related codices of Snorri's Edda for the Skáldskaparmál hair-myth and the Gylfaginning genealogy that names Ullr her son. No certain place-name contains her name, though the root sif- is bound up with ordinary words for kinship across the Germanic languages; and while the Younger Futhark rendering ᛋᛁᚠ is unambiguous, no Viking-Age carving of the theonym has ever been read. The material afterlife of her myth is real but indirect: the treasures her shearing produced — Mjölnir above all — are among the most depicted objects of the Viking Age, worn as amulets in thousands of graves, so that the consequence of her one great scene is archaeologically everywhere while she herself is nowhere.

**Exhibit 4 — the continuing record.** Sif's afterlife runs on two tracks, one scholarly and one popular.  In the scholarly line she is the type-case of the Edda's reticence about goddesses: a figure with no cult record and one great myth, whose golden hair made her, from Grimm onward, the default Germanic corn-goddess of the comparative handbooks, and whose name — plain sif, 'affinity' — became the standing example of a theonym that is simply an abstract noun.

## The Convention's Own History

The canonical spelling of **Sif** rests on the tradition's own scholarly record, not on a marks convention: the name's forms are documented, compared, and one reference spelling is fixed so that citations agree across the temple, the lexicon, and this register. The principle that unifies every entry is the one the whole project stands on: a name is evidence, and evidence is not negotiable — not for keyboards, not for convenience, not for anyone.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Sif** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

## The Verdict

Case closed on **Sif**: canonical, cited, and defended. The keyboard form *sif* is the same name in another register of display — always acceptable. The register's files remain open: if a source surfaces that changes any line of this entry, the entry changes. Until then, the temple at [/sif/](/sif/) holds the canonical form.

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 6 cited sources — Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál (the shearing of Sif's hair; the sons of Ívaldi and the making of the golden hair, Gungnir, and Skíðblaðnir; Loki's wager with Brokkr and the forging of Draupnir, Gullinbursti, and Mjölnir; kennings for Þórr as 'husband of Sif'); Gylfaginning 32 (Ullr son of Sif, stepson of Þórr), trans. Anthony Faulkes, Poetic Edda: Lokasenna 53–54 (Sif pours the crystal cup; Loki's accusation); Hárbarðsljóð 48 ('Sif has a lover at home'), trans. Carolyne Larrington, Cleasby–Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary s.v. sif, sifjar; de Vries, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch s.v. sif (the kinship etymology: Old Norse sif, Old English sibb, Old High German sippa).
